item.title: A beginners guide to visiting Ketchikan by cruise ship
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
A beginners guide to visiting Ketchikan by cruise ship Located just north of the Canadian border, Ketchikan is the southernmost city in Alaska. Founded in August of 1900, Ketchikan is situated on Revillagigedo Island near the Tongass Narrows, the entrance to the Pacific Ocean and the famed Inside Passage. A historic fishing village with a long-standing Tlingit Native presence, today Ketchikan still represents both of these separate worlds while catering to tourists at the same time. In fact, Ketchikan has the world's largest collection of totem poles spread across four major sites, the most recognizable being Totem Bight State Park. Since the city is perched on stilts, much of Ketchikan's downtown sits high above the water. This is particularly prominent in the historic Creek Street district that runs parallel to Ketchikan Creek. Once the town's Red Light district, Creek Street now hosts tourist shops and, in the fall months, it's a prime spot to view salmon as they come upstream to spawn. Ketchikan is also noteworthy for its proximity to Misty Fjords National Monument, offering numerous flightseeing excursions and wildlife boat tours to this pristine section of the Tongass National Forest. Known as one of the "big three" Alaska ports of call (together with Juneau and Skagway), Ketchikan is a featured stop on most cruises to the state. Just remember to bring your umbrella when you visit — the city is in the heart of a rainforest and gets about 232 days of rain per year. There's even a "rain gauge" near the main cruise pier that shows how much rain Ketchikan has had so far this year. - The historic Creek Street district for both activities and views. - Opportunities to explore both in town and nearby attractions, such as Misty Fjords and the Tongass National Forest. - An abundance of local Tlingit culture. - It can be a hike to walk from Berth 4 to the heart of town. - Some ships owned by Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings (Norwegian, Oceania and Regent Seven Seas) dock at the more far-flung Ward Cove – a 20-minute drive from Ketchikan proper. - If you're going to see rain in Alaska, it's going to be here (definitely, bring, and don your rain gear). Ships calling on Ketchikan tie up in the heart of downtown, directly across from most of the city's bars, restaurants and shops, and just a few minutes' walk from historic Creek Street. Ketchikan has four berths,numbered 1 to 4. Berths 1 and 2 are just steps away from the shops at Salmon Landing and attractions like The Great Alaskan Lumberjack Show, while Berth 3 is situated near the long-standing Tongass Trading Company shop right on the harbor. Berth 4, the most distant, is about a 10- to 15-minute walk from the heart of downtown. Passengers arriving to Ketchikan onboard Norwegian Cruise Line, Oceania or Regent Seven Seas ships will dock at Ward Cove, a new cruise terminal area designed in conjunction with Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings, situated approximately 20 minute's drive west of Ketchikan. There are free shuttle buses to take passengers into downtown Ketchikan, with a drop-off point adjacent to Berth 4. While this area is closer to some of the outdoor shore excursion activities and does contain several shops at the terminal – itself housed in an old cannery – it does require more patience to get into the heart of Ketchikan. Language: English is the official language in Ketchikan. Currency: The U.S. dollar is used for all purchases in Ketchikan. Time zone: Ketchikan is in the Alaska Time Zone (GMT-8), one hour behind Pacific Standard Time and four hours behind Eastern Standard Time. Top things to do in Ketchikan cruise port Ketchikan offers a plethora of ways to spend your day. You can stroll the quaint streets and do a little window shopping and sample the superb seafood on offer, choose to get acquainted with the city's extensive Tlingit native history or venture father afield to places like nearby Misty Fjords for scenic wildlife cruises or flightseeing. Families would do well to check out The Great Alaskan Lumberjack Show. This reasonably priced entertainment venue offers fun for the whole family with plenty of showmanship as performers race up tall logs, engage in carving and axe-throwing competitions and try their best to stay upright in the log rolling competition. While the event is outdoors, sheltered and heated seating keeps guests comfortable. No visit to Ketchikan is complete without a visit to Totem Bight State Park, one of four locations in Ketchikan where these magnificent works of art are on display. The Totem Heritage Center offers a great collection of Tlingit and Haida totems, and it's a manageable stroll from town for those looking to visit independently. Totem Bight and Saxman Totem Park are best explored as part of a shore excursion due to their relatively far distance from town. Creek Street, just a 10-minute walk from the majority of the cruise piers, attracts throngs of tourists, even in the rain. This former red-light district is now a shopping mecca that also offers excellent views of spawning salmon (and the odd harbor seal). Be sure to stop in at Dolly's House, a former brothel turned into a museum. Outside of town, Misty Fjords National Monument is an excellent choice for wildlife and nature cruises that depart from Ketchikan. Hiking is also a popular option in Ketchikan. The trailheads for both Perseverance Lake and Frog Pond are near the Ward Cove docks, convenient for adventurers whose ships dock there. While Alaska shore excursions can be jaw-droppingly expensive, Ketchikan is one of the few ports that seems to have an excellent balance between relatively inexpensive excursions that last only a few hours and longer, more expensive bucket-list trips like crab feasts and wildlife cruises. If you're a fan of the long-running Discovery Channel show, "The Deadliest Catch," you'll be happy to know you can actually set out on one of the ships featured in the show. The Aleutian Ballad, featured in Season 2, has been converted into a tourist attraction that sails into the Inside Passage, giving guests a glimpse at what it takes to handle the massive king crab pots and endure life on the Bering Sea. There are a number of different pairings for the Great Alaskan Lumberjack Show, including excursions that pair it with a crab feast; axe-throwing experience; or a visit to Totem Bight State Park. Either way, it is one of the most affordable and surprisingly enjoyable family-friendly experiences in Alaska. Wilderness exploration cruise and crab feast This four-hour excursion packs in a cruise of the wilderness setting of nearby George Inlet, where wildlife is abundant (the best eagle sightings I've ever seen have been here). That, naturally, is paired with an all-you-can-eat Dungeness crab feast at the George Inlet Lodge. How much crab can one person eat? Find out on this absolutely indulgent excursion. It's kitschy and often groan-inducing, but exploring Ketchikan by amphibious duck boat has been a staple of excursions here for decades. Inexpensive, informative and good for the whole family, it makes for a fascinating tour of Ketchikan by land and sea. On foot: This is the best way to see Ketchikan, as much of the town is accessible within walking distance for most people. Those with mobility issues might want to opt for panoramic tours with several stops, particularly if docking at Ward Cove. Taxi: As with most Alaskan cities and towns, taxis are available here but can be difficult to come by, particularly when ships are in port. Services like Uber and Lyft are available, but they can also be expensive and hard to find. Bike or scooter: It is possible to rent bicycles or e-bikes from several providers in Ketchikan that can be useful for getting around town. Car: Car rentals are not widely available in Ketchikan. Ketchikan restaurants near the cruise pier Ketchikan has a number of great restaurants for cruise passengers to indulge in, and they should. The seafood served here is fantastic, and restaurants run the gamut from small grab-and-go shops to venues with harbor views. Look for eateries serving down-home comfort food if you need a refreshing change from the fare on your ship. Our go-to spot is the Alaska Fish House, which is just steps from Berth 1 and adjacent to the Great Alaskan Lumberjack Show. The salmon chowder here is to die for, and the venue has indoor and outdoor seating — not to mention a variety of local Alaskan beers on tap. If that's full, consider Ketchikan Crab & Go, conveniently located next door, inside the shops at Salmon Landing. It also offers plenty of indoor and outdoor seating. Other standouts in Ketchikan include The Krabby Krab Shack on Main Street (a welcome addition to the Ketchikan dining scene); The Pioneer Cafe on Mission Street for diner-style, uncomplicated but delicious eats; Timber & Tide, one of the few establishments right at Berth 4; and the always-popular New York Cafe on Stedman Street, a few blocks past the main entrance to Creek Street. As you might have guessed, salmon has played an enormous role in shaping Ketchikan's history. Salmon is also our top recommendation to try here, from chowder to rolls to burgers. You can also get more than enough Alaskan crab and other seafood here, too. For those who aren't seafood mavens, fear not: Ketchikan has a surprising variety of culinary options, from standard American fare to Mexican, Asian and European-inspired dishes. You don't have to look far to find shopping options, no matter where you're docked in Ketchikan. Shops line the length of Front Street along Ketchikan's berths, and even Ward Cove has its own dedicated shopping area inside the former cannery that now serves as a cruise terminal and welcome center. Tongass Trading Co., near Berth 3, is a Ketchikan staple that caters to tourists and locals alike. The Shops at Salmon Landing, located across from Berth 1, have been offering tourists plenty of opportunities to spend money since their debut in the 1990s. But if you walk a few blocks into the town of Ketchikan, away from Front Street, you'll find more authentic, local shops filled with arts, crafts and more. Creek Street, too, is filled with shops — some touristic, some local, some chintzy, some expensive. Literary fans will want to stop into Parnassus Books, while those looking for authentic Native art will want to call on Crazy Wolf Studio, just up the street on Mission. Free things to do in the Ketchikan cruise port It costs nothing to visit Ketchikan's historic Creek Street neighborhood. There are entrances to its boardwalk from both Dock Street (near Parnassus Books) and Stedman Street (near the New York Cafe). Take a stroll from Creek Street along Married Man's Trail up into the heart of Ketchikan's upper town, particularly when the salmon are running, for some great nature views. A salmon ladder observation platform is at the top of Married Man's Trail and is worth the visit. While not entirely free, you can take the Cape Fox Lodge Funicular from the base of Creek Street up to the Cape Fox Lodge for a small fee. (Those dining at the Lodge's restaurant have the funicular fee waived.) Closed for six years, the funicular just reopened in the summer of 2025 and offers spectacular views. Travelers with kids might want to take an easy 15-minute stroll from Ketchikan's Berth 1, near Salmon Landing, to the excellent Totem Heritage Playground, just steps from the equally worthwhile Totem Heritage Center (a small entry fee applies for the latter). Included on nearly every cruise itinerary to Alaska, Ketchikan is a wonderful port where visitors can wander around town or explore the vibrant nature that surrounds the city. Just don't forget your umbrella.

item.title: 7 wonders of Greece: from hot springs frequented by Aristotle to the magical Meteora monasteries
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
It’s hard to find only seven wonders when it comes to Greece. With Europe’s longest coastline strewn with bleached blonde sands, secret coves and bijou harbours where brightly coloured kaiki fishing boats bob at anchor next to waterside tavernas serving seafood fresh from the net, it’s hardly surprising that Greece is a magnet for beach-lovers and sunseekers, but also history buffs and foodies always looking for new culinary delights to discover. I've long adored Greece, and I can't wait to be back on my next trip, whether that'll be spent relaxing for the week by the sea in Paros, hikes and cycling adventures in Crete, or days spent hopping between galleries and restaurants in Athens. But away from the (admittedly hard to resist) lure of mirror-clear seas and sumptuous strands, there’s plenty more to discover in this spellbinding southeastern European country, which stretches from culturally rich Macedonia in the north to the rugged landscapes and pristine seascapes of the Peloponnese peninsula in the south. Beyond the familiar postcard scenes lie ancient monasteries perched on seemingly impossible cliffs, remarkable feats of engineering and archaeological treasures hidden beneath the waves. From ancient shipwrecks to mineral-rich springs that have been drawing visitors for centuries, these are seven wonders of Greece that deserve a place on your itinerary. With its triangular sections like giant sails, the world’s longest multi-span cable-stayed bridge seems to float above the wave-riffled waters of the vast Rion Strait like a magnificent ship. Bridging the 2,880-metre-long gap between the town of Rio on the Peloponnese peninsula and Antirrio in mainland Greece, this miracle of modern engineering, which took five years to build and cost around €800 million, was finally opened in 2004. Once upon a time, it took 50 minutes to cross the strait in a ferry; nowadays, you can whizz back and forth between the Peloponnese and mainland Greece in minutes. You’ll probably want to drive at a dawdling pace, however, because the views over the strait’s indigo depths to the mighty mountain ranges beyond are almost as spectacular as the bridge itself. Stand on one of the banks of the Corinth Canal watching a boat passing through the impossibly narrow, 21.3-metre-wide cleft between sheer limestone rock walls, and you can’t fail to be wowed by this mammoth project that involved cutting through several kilometres of solid rock. Back in the 7th century BC, when notorious tyrant Periander first conceived his idea of creating a pathway between the Ionian and Aegean Seas, he was considered crazy. Over the centuries, historical figures including the Roman emperors Caligula and Nero toyed with the idea – in 67 AD, Emperor Nero set a team of thousands of labourers to work on the mammoth task, but the project was abandoned following his death in 68 AD. Work finally began in 1882, and after a slew of financial and technical issues, the 6.4-kilometre canal connecting the Gulf of Corinth with the Saronic Gulf opened in 1893. Following months of closure for landslide prevention and restoration works, the canal reopened to navigation in June 2026, allowing smaller vessels and tourist boats to once again make the spectacular passage between its towering walls. For a more adventurous way to see it up close, you can even do a bungee jump. Starting south of Kalamata and stretching to Cape Tainaron, the fabled entrance to the Underworld, the Mani sits on the middle digit of the Peloponnese. Backed by the mighty Taygetus mountains, the thyme-spiked landscapes of this rugged region, which remained relatively isolated until the expansion of its road network in the 20th century, are dotted with pyrgospita, unique stone towers as narrow as church belfries, where belligerent locals hid out as they flung cannonballs at each other during the endless feuds that rocked these hillsides for centuries. With feuds long gone, you should explore picturesque pyrgospita villages such as Vathia or Pyrgos, sample smoked pork sygklino, myzithra cheese and other traditional treats in the taverna tower of Barba Petros, and then spend the night in your very own pyrgospiti, hopefully without throwing cannonballs at your neighbours. For centuries, visitors have flocked to the seaside resort of Edipsos on Evia’s northern gulf to wallow in mineral-rich spring waters, long celebrated for their therapeutic properties. The town's bathing tradition dates back to antiquity, with famous visitors over the years including Aristotle and Maria Callas. Bubbling out of the ground at temperatures that can reach 80°C, hot springs criss-cross the entire town: streaming through the centre in narrow canals, or gushing in steaming waterfalls from cliffs near the beach. Where the thermal waters meet the cooler sea, visitors can enjoy a natural open-air bathing experience. If you fancy a tad more luxury, there are several hotels that have harnessed the hot waters. The best is grand dame hotel Thermae Sylla, which has an award-winning medical spa complex with indoor and outdoor spring-fed pools. Home to the Mediterranean’s first underwater museum, Alonissos is one of the remotest islands of the Sporades island chain, which includes Mamma Mia island, Skopelos and party-loving Skiathos. Greece’s so-called ‘Parthenon of shipwrecks’ is a merchant vessel that sank off this coastline with several thousand wine amphorae on board sometime in the fifth century BC. It lies some 25 metres down, beneath glass-clear waters in Alonissos’ 2,260 sq km national marine park where endangered monk seals find refuge. Opened to visitors in 2020, the underwater museum allows certified divers to explore the ancient wreck alongside experienced guides. You'll need an Advanced Open Water Diver qualification to take the plunge, but those who prefer to stay on dry land can discover the shipwreck through a virtual experience at the Visitor Information Centre in Patitiri. Away from those mesmerising waters, grab a seat at Hayiati, a cliff-perched café in island capital Hora’s cobbled streets where they serve delicious cinnamon-dusted galatopita milk pie. One of my favourite Greek islands, Lesvos, has plenty of hidden gems, but the Teriade Museum, in the village of Varia, just outside Mytilene, is the one not to miss. Teriade, who studied art in Paris, rubbed shoulders with many of the 20th century’s greatest artists, and he managed to persuade them to collaborate with him on his celebrated art publication, Verve, which he published from 1937 right up to 1960. The museum's collection includes beautifully illustrated artists' books, original prints and works by Chagall, Picasso, Matisse and other 20th-century ‘greats’. In any major city, this museum would be packed; in Lesvos, you’ll probably have it almost all to yourself. It’s hardly surprising that the magical Meteora monasteries have inspired filmmakers and artists alike, with their extraordinary landscape even providing the backdrop for the Eyrie in Game of Thrones: perched on top of their lofty stone pinnacles, these medieval sanctuaries rise out of Thessaly’s dramatic landscape like colossal sponge fingers. The six monasteries, whose name derives from the Greek word meaning 'suspended in the air', are among Greece's most extraordinary UNESCO World Heritage Sites. While they can get busy during the summer months, particularly with day-trippers from Athens, visiting early in the morning or outside peak season offers a quieter experience. Kalambaka, the town at the foot of the towering rocks, is around a four-hour drive from the capital. It’s well worth making the effort to visit, however, for the thrill of visiting Agia Triada (Holy Trinity), which starred in the 1981 James Bond film For Your Eyes Only, or seeing the historic hoisting mechanisms once used to transport monks and supplies up to Moni Varlaam, a 16th-century monastery perched on a precipitous cinnamon-coloured swirl of rock which is now reached by clambering up 195 steps.

item.title: It’s officially flu season: Here's how to avoid getting sick on a plane
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
It’s officially flu season: Here's how to avoid getting sick on a plane It's officially that time of year. Temperatures are dropping, hot tea is flowing and flu season is here in full force. But that's not the only illness looming over travelers this holiday season. According to Dr. Waleed Javaid, epidemiologist and professor of medicine at West Virginia University, "Currently, there is a mix of respiratory illnesses, including COVID-19, influenza and RSV (respiratory syncytial virus). Other common illnesses include norovirus and bacterial infections like E. coli. As we enter the colder months and holiday gatherings, respiratory infections are on the rise due to increased close contact and indoor activities." Thankfully, we learned much about mitigating sickness while traveling during the COVID-19 pandemic. "COVID taught us the importance of hand hygiene and boosting immunity through lifestyle practices," said Dr. Taz Bhatia, a board-certified integrative medicine physician and medical adviser to the cold and flu medicine brand Genexa. Many precautions you learned to stop the spread of COVID-19 should also help protect you from seasonal influenza, according to Healthline (which is owned by TPG's parent company, Red Ventures). The last thing you want is to catch a bug on a plane and be miserable for the rest of your vacation. To protect yourself — and your family — from catching the flu and other illnesses while traveling, follow these tips. Though the days of mandatory face coverings on flights are over, wearing one can still help prevent you from getting sick. A 2020 study by the U.S. Department of Defense found the risk of COVID-19 transmission on a plane was "extremely unlikely" when masks were worn. Masks will also help protect you from other common respiratory viruses, like influenza, that are transmitted through the air. Currently, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends the use of masks for sick travelers (with fever or respiratory symptoms) to help reduce the spread of respiratory germs, and for people sitting near sick travelers (with fever or respiratory symptoms) when the patient cannot tolerate wearing a mask. We all know that washing our hands is key to preventing sickness, but it's especially true when traveling. "Keep your hands clean," said Dr. Nicholas Testa, California regional chief medical officer at CommonSpirit Health. "This means a combination of good hand hygiene with either soap and water or an alcohol-based hand sanitizer." According to the CDC, hand washing is the "single most important infection control measure." It recommends using "alcohol-based hand sanitizer (containing at least 60% alcohol) if soap and water are not available." If it's a short flight, make sure you go to the bathroom before your flight takes off, New York-based primary care physician Dr. Marina Gafanovich told TPG. Why? "You have to understand that many people are sharing that bathroom," she said. "And research suggests that there are significant germs on sinks, flush handles and toilet seats on airplane bathrooms. That is why it's best to use paper towels when you touch the toilet seat or faucet or even the door latch." While a comfortable indoor humidity level is anywhere from 30% to 65%, the humidity inside an airplane cabin is only around 10% to 20%, according to Northwestern Medicine. This can dry out the mucous membranes of your nose and airways, making them much more susceptible to viruses and bacteria. To combat this, stay hydrated. "Bring your own bottle of water and aim to drink eight ounces of water per hour you're in the air to maintain your hydration," said Dr. Nate Favini, the chief medical officer at Pair Team, a virtual care company. "Alcohol and caffeine will dehydrate you even more, so save the cocktails and coffee for your destination." In addition to washing your hands, be cognizant of those areas on a plane that are particularly high-touch surfaces. The flu virus, for example, can live on any hard surface for up to 24 hours. "Don't use the tray table and, if you really have to, make sure you carry sanitary wipes with you and clean it before you use it," said Gafanovich. "Also, don't store items in the seatback pocket. We know many people use it, so it's likely to be full of germs." Testa also recommends avoiding or wiping down overhead air vents, lavatory flush buttons and seat belt buckles. So, be sure to stock up on hand sanitizing wipes before your next flight. Stick with classics like Purell, or try these wipes designed specifically for travelers. And if you just want to spray your hands (or everything), try Dr. Bronner's lavender-scented organic hand sanitizer spray in TSA-friendly bottles. No matter how clean your hands are, it's best to keep them away from your face, too. "Even if your hands have touched the dirtiest, germiest surfaces, you won't get sick from that unless you bring those germs to a point of entry (nose, mouth, eyes)," said Florida-based internist Dr. Frank Contacessa. "Get in the habit of never rubbing your eyes, touching your mouth or your nose unless you just washed your hands. This is one of the greatest ways to avoid getting sick." Just can't kick the habit of touching your face? Try gloves. Dr. Julie Fischer, an associate research professor in the department of microbiology and immunology at Georgetown University, told TPG, "Gloves are useful in that they remind people not to touch their own noses and mouth ... when you're wearing gloves, you become hyper-conscious of that. But the best protection for individuals is to be very careful about handwashing." Studies have shown that the aisle seats on an airplane experience significantly more traffic and run a greater risk of exposure. Why? In part, sick patients tend to brace themselves on those seats when walking to the bathroom. "The window seat is a better selection if you want to minimize the risk of respiratory transmission," said Testa. These seats generally don't have as much contact with passengers. While you might think that sitting in recycled air for hours could increase your risk of illness, keeping your air vent on may actually help. "There's been some research that showed that using the overhead air vent, directed straight downward, can create a cone of protection," said Contacessa. "It can actually prevent airborne germs from getting close to you. The airflow from the vent can help to ward off another passenger's sneeze germs." In fact, high-efficiency particulate air, or HEPA, filters on planes remove at least 99.97% of airborne viruses and bacteria. That air is also refreshed about 20 times per hour, whereas air in a typical office only gets refreshed about 10 times. Before you even set foot on a plane, you can start preventive measures to avoid getting sick. The CDC recommends staying updated on vaccinations, including annual flu shots, COVID-19 boosters and RSV vaccines for those eligible, to minimize the risk of severe illness. In addition, "Prioritize sleep, a balanced diet, and supplements like vitamin D and zinc," said Bhatia. It's also worth packing vitamin C. "Studies have shown that people under stress who take 1,000 milligrams of vitamin C per day are less likely to fall ill with viral infections," said Favini. "And travel is often stressful." Even though the worst of the COVID-19 pandemic is long gone, staying healthy when traveling is still important. The above tips can help minimize your risk this flu season so you can make the most of your holiday travels. When stocking up on supplements, hand wipes and other supplies, don't forget that some credit cards earn bonus points at drugstores or grocery stores. item.title: JetBlue announces first-class upgrades, new elite benefits for 2027
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
JetBlue announces first-class upgrades, new elite benefits for 2027 - All JetBlue Mosaic elites will be eligible for complimentary domestic first-class upgrades - Some Mosaic members can also earn confirmable upgrade certificates, redeemable in the Mint or BlueFirst cabins - New "Perks You Pick" available, including lounge passes JetBlue is just weeks away from launching service in its new domestic first-class cabin. And with those "BlueFirst" seats now on sale, the carrier is offering some long-promised details about what upgrades will look like for elite status members. All TrueBlue Mosaic members will be eligible for unlimited complimentary upgrades to the first-class cabin — when seats are available, of course. That's on par with the upgrade policies at other full-service U.S. carriers. Flyers who carry the JetBlue Premier Card, the carrier's premium credit card, will also be eligible. The information for the JetBlue Premier Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Heading into 2027, JetBlue is also revamping the confirmable upgrade certificates members can earn as they climb the status ladder. Plus, there are some changes to the choice perks TrueBlue members can claim, known as "Perks You Pick." Many of these changes will take effect Feb. 1. However, upgrades into BlueFirst will begin as soon as those seats start appearing on planes. Here's what to know. First things first, JetBlue won't change the elite status qualification requirements. In 2027, TrueBlue members will need the same number of "tiles" to reach the four Mosaic tiers. As always, travelers can earn tiles (JetBlue's status metric) a few ways, including by flying and spending on eligible cobranded credit cards. First-class upgrades on JetBlue: What to know The biggest change to JetBlue Mosaic status in 2027 involves upgrades. That's thanks to the debut of BlueFirst, which is slated to start appearing on the first planes in December. The new front cabin will allow the airline to introduce complimentary, space-available upgrades to its loyalty members for the first time. How complimentary BlueFirst upgrades will work JetBlue passengers eligible for upgrades can clear the queue up to an hour before departure. When there are empty seats, here is how the upgrade priority will shake out: - JetBlue Premier cardholders without status A few additional points to know: - Mosaic members will be allowed one companion who can upgrade into BlueFirst, too. - Travelers who book "base" (basic) main cabin or EvenMore fares will not be eligible for an upgrade. - JetBlue Premier cardholders without status must pay for their trip with their JetBlue Premier card to be eligible for a BlueFirst upgrade. Which planes will get BlueFirst? JetBlue plans to install the domestic-style BlueFirst cabin on all of its planes that don't have Mint (its lie-flat, business-class cabin). The airline will not offer standard complimentary upgrades into Mint. High-level TrueBlue status members will also have the option to confirm an upgrade after booking a flight. Historically, JetBlue has offered higher-tier Mosaic members an allotment of "Move to Mint" certificates that were good for a spot in the airline's long-haul business cabin. Going forward, "Move to Mint" will be rebranded as "Premium Upgrade Certificates," which travelers can use in either Mint or BlueFirst. - Mosaic 3 members automatically receive four Premium Upgrade Certificates upon reaching 150 tiles. - Mosaic 4 members automatically receive four additional certificates upon hitting 250 tiles. Members can select additional Premium Upgrade Certificates from JetBlue's menu of "Perks You Pick." That option begins at Mosaic 2. How many Premium Upgrade Certificates for a seat? JetBlue's Premium Upgrade Certificates can be applied any time after booking, up to two hours before departure. As always, redeeming upgrade certificates is subject to availability. The number of certificates you'll need for a confirmed upgrade will fluctuate dynamically from one flight to another, as shown in the carrier's published graphic. Beyond upgrades, JetBlue revamped its menu of "Perks You Pick." These are the additional, optional benefits that members unlock as they gain higher status. New additions to the list include one-time passes to JetBlue's new BlueHouse lounges in New York City and Boston (only top-tier Mosaic 4 status unlocks a full lounge membership). Plus, the carrier is offering some new exclusive perk options for its Premier cardholders. Some details that are important to know: - You get one pick at each tile threshold. - JetBlue will now allow you to choose a benefit more than once. A few past Perks You Pick will disappear in 2027, including: - $99 statement credit on eligible JetBlue credit cards - Pet fee waiver (That will now become a signature perk starting at Mosaic 2 status) Related reading:

item.title: Sweet Potato Casserole
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Some say the best sweet potato casserole is covered in marshmallows; others swear by a buttery streusel or toasty maple-slicked pecans. While I firmly believe crunchy contrast is essential to this classic Thanksgiving side dish, thereâs one small problem: Iâm allergic to nuts. My sweet potato casserole recipe swaps the nuts for crispy, sweet-and-salty cornflakesâthe marshmallows can stay. Tossed with melted butter, brown sugar, cinnamon, and salt, the cornflakes turn golden and crunchy in the oven. Add a handful of chopped pecans if you must, but trust me, you wonât miss them. Instead of boiling the spuds or reaching for canned sweet potatoes, I roast fresh ones until tender, concentrating their flavor instead of washing it down the drain. For the silkiest purÃ©e, skip the potato masher and give the cooked sweet potatoes a whiz in the food processor. Can you make sweet potato casserole ahead of time? Yes. Get a head start by roasting the sweet potatoes up to 3 days in advance. Let them cool, then cover and refrigerate until youâre ready to make the casserole. Add the cornflakes and marshmallows just before baking, so the topping stays crisp. For more ways to get ahead of the holiday rush, browse our make-ahead Thanksgiving recipes. Can you make sweet potato casserole without marshmallows? Sure. The brown-sugar-coated cornflakes bring plenty of sweetness and crunch on their own. Simply skip the marshmallows and scatter the cornflakes evenly over the purÃ©e. Watch the topping as it bakes so it doesnât get too dark. Or try our savory sweet potato casserole, with brown butter, rosemary, and crisp breadcrumbs in place of the sweet topping. Is this sweet potato casserole gluten-free? It can be. Some cornflakes contain malt syrup or malt extract, made from barley, so they arenât gluten-free. Check the box and choose a certified gluten-free cereal if needed. Are yams the same thing as sweet potatoes? Technically, no. Botanically, yams and sweet potatoes are entirely different vegetables, but in parts of the US, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes might be labeled âyams.â Confused? Read more: - Stainless Steel Mixing Bowls, Set of 6 $39 $36 At Amazon Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Preheat oven to 350Â°. Place 3 lb. sweet potatoes (about 3 large), peeled, cut into 1" pieces, in a 13x9" baking dish or on a foil-lined baking sheet. Cover with foil and bake until tender, 50â60 minutes. Do Ahead: Sweet potatoes can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill. Step 2Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, Â¼ cup half-and-half, Â¼ cup (packed; 50 g) dark brown sugar, Â¼ cup (Â½ stick) unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1Â¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Step 3Transfer half of sweet potatoes to a food processor, add half of egg mixture, and process until smooth, about 2 minutes. Transfer purÃ©e to a large mixing bowl. Repeat with remaining sweet potatoes and egg mixture. Scrape all of purÃ©e into baking dish (no need to clean). Step 4Combine 2 cups cornflakes, 1 tsp. ground cinnamon, remaining Â¼ cup (packed; 50 g) dark brown sugar, remaining Â¼ cup (Â½ stick) unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and remaining 1Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large resealable plastic bag, seal, and shake to coat cereal. Step 5Arrange cornflake mixture and marshmallows over top of purÃ©e in alternating diagonal stripes. Bake casserole until marshmallows are golden brown, 25â30 minutes. item.title: How Long to Cook a Turkey by Weight
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Several factors contribute to a perfect Thanksgiving, but the holiday hinges on one question in particular: How long will it take to cook that turkey? Notoriously prone to overcooking, turkey meat has been ridiculed for its perceived dryness time and again. On top of the meatâs naturally lean characteristics, these very large birds have sections that vary widely in shape and thickness, making it tough (pun intended) to achieve a juicy interior and crispy, golden-brown skin. Sadly, not even the richest turkey gravy can save a bird that isnât cooked properly. So, how long does it take to cook a turkey? For a whole, unstuffed turkey, plan on roughly 13 minutes per pound at 350Â°F. That works out to about 3 hours for a 12- to 14-pound bird, though the precise roasting time depends on its size, your oven temperature, and how you prepare it. But that doesnât mean it has to take up all of your prep time. Armed with the turkey-cooking time chart below and a few essential roasting tips, youâll have ample time to focus on arguably everyoneâs favorite part of the Thanksgiving dinner spread (the side dishes) without stressing too much about the main event. The simplest approach is to roast a whole, unstuffed turkey, breast-side up, at 350Â°F. Ideal for first-time turkey cooks, this method requires relatively little attention and results in an excellent bird. As a general rule, allow about 13 minutes per pound, but keep in mind that cooking times are only estimates. Use the chart below to determine approximately how long your turkey will need in the oven: These times assume your turkey is fully thawed and unstuffed. Start checking for doneness about three-quarters of the way through the estimated roasting time, then check more frequently as the turkey approaches its target temperature. Remember, the thermometerânot the clockâgets the final say. One more thing: Stuffed turkeys take much longer to cook through, making the breast meat prone to drying out while you wait for the center of the stuffing to reach a safe temperature. We prefer stuffing recipes (a.k.a. dressing recipes) that bake separately. A perfectly browned bird isnât necessarily a fully cooked one. The most reliable way to check for doneness is with an instant-read thermometer, inserted into the thickest part of the breast and the innermost portions of the thigh, without touching bone. The USDA recommends cooking turkey to an internal temperature of 165Â°F in all three spots. Food director Chris Morocco recommends cooking dark meat to an even higher final temperatureâaround 175Â°â190Â°Fâso its connective tissue has more time to break down. Thatâs part of what makes cooking a whole turkey tricky: The breast and legs donât reach their ideal temperatures at the same time. Youâll also want to account for carryover cooking. A turkeyâs internal temperature keeps rising after it comes out of the oven because of residual heat. Some of our favorite roast turkey recipes use that residual heat to finish cooking the meat, but the temperature increase varies with the size of the bird and the roasting method; donât assume it will rise by a specific number of degrees. The Bon AppÃ©tit Test Kitchen recommends removing your turkey from the oven when the breast has reached an internal temperature of 150Â°F. Check the temperature periodically while the bird rests to ensure it reaches 165Â°F. Before you start carving, give your turkey a rest. For a whole bird, 30â60 minutes allows the juices to redistribute, helping keep the meat moist when you cut into it. Set the turkey on a cutting board with a trough or a platter to collect any runoff juices (save them for gravy). You donât need to tent it with aluminum foil: the birdâs insulation will keep it warm surprisingly long. Plus, trapping steam beneath the foil can cause crispy skin to go limp. Whether you roast your turkey whole, spatchcocked, or cut into parts, take these preliminary steps. They wonât necessarily shorten the cooking time, but theyâll help you get that succulent-on-the-inside, crackly-on-the-outside result. Unless you look forward to eating leftover turkey for days, shop for a bird thatâs just big enough to feed your Thanksgiving crew. A smaller turkey will cut roasting time, leaving the oven free for sides and pies. A frozen turkey needs time to thawâand not just a few hours on the counter. Plan on about 24 hours in the refrigerator for every 4â5 pounds of turkey. That means a 12- to 14-pound bird will need roughly three to four days to thaw completely. A partially frozen turkey can seriously throw off your roasting time, and without thawing, you may not be able to remove the giblets. If Thanksgiving is approaching faster than your bird is defrosting, there are other safe ways to speed things along. Dry brining is key to moist, succulent meat. Whether you choose plain kosher salt, a salt-and-pepper mix, or a custom spice blend, salt draws moisture to the turkeyâs surface. The salty juices are then reabsorbed into the meat, carrying the seasoning with them. This helps the turkey retain moisture as it cooks, tenderizes the meat, and encourages skin browningâall hallmarks of a properly cooked bird. What about a wet brine, you ask? Weâre firmly in the dry-brine camp. Itâs easier, less messy, and doesnât require finding space in an already crowded refrigerator for a giant container of salt water. (Fridge space is at a premium leading up to Thanksgiving.) Give your dry-brined turkey at least 12 hours and up to three days in the refrigerator, uncovered, before roasting. That might sound lengthy, but the salt needs time to work its way through the turkeyâs big muscles. If youâre running behind, you can start dry-brining before the bird has completely thawed. Once the exterior is pliable enough to season, apply the brine and return the turkey to the refrigerator to finish thawing. Invest in an oven thermometer before the big day arrives. Oven temperatures can vary from what the dial shows, and even a small discrepancy can make a difference when youâre roasting something for several hours. Once the turkey is in the oven, resist the urge to keep checking on it. Opening the door lets heat escape, which can lengthen cooking time. A thermometer and a little patience will serve you better than peeking at the bird repeatedly. This method comes from Andy Baraghaniâs dry-brined roast turkey recipe (a.k.a. the no-fail turkey method we come back to every Thanksgiving). Andy had two main goals for his perfect turkey: brown the skin so itâs crackly and delicious, and roast the meat so itâs tender and moist. The secret to accomplishing both? Two oven temperatures. Andy starts his turkey at relatively high heatâ425Â°â450Â°F for 30â45 minutesâto encourage browning, then reduces the temperature to 300Â°â350Â°F for another 65â85 minutes, following the recipeâs internal-temperature guidance. As a bonus, he brushes the outside of the bird with a tangy honey glaze to build a glossy, bronzed shellac. This two-temperature method can get a 12- to 16-pound turkey out of the oven in around two hours, considerably faster than the standard approach. Youâll have to pay closer attention, though: Keep an eye on the skin, and follow the recipeâs instructions for adjusting the heat if it starts to get too dark. For the full technique, including the dry brine and glaze, follow Andyâs recipe. Roasting a turkey in parts is another way to address uneven cooking. With the pieces arranged separately, each one gets optimal exposure to the ovenâs heat, giving you more control over when the breast and dark meat are done. And yes, even turkey pieces benefit from a dry brine, so the preparation tips above still apply. You can break down the raw turkey yourself if you feel confident (and have a sharp enough knife), but thereâs no shame in asking your butcher to handle the job. Request five pieces: two legs, two wings, and one whole turkey breast, with the backbone removed. Save that backbone for turkey stock. Instead of a typical roasting pan, this method uses a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet. The setup lets hot air circulate around the meat, giving the skin its best chance to crisp while catching the umami-packed drippings. In another favorite Thanksgiving turkey recipe, the dry-brined pieces roast at 425Â°F for 20â25 minutes, then 300Â°F for another 50â70 minutes. Cooking in parts lets you can monitor each piece individually, so you can pull the breast when it reaches the right temperature and give the legs more time if needed. Follow the recipeâs instructions for assessing doneness, keeping in mind the USDAâs 165Â°F minimum temperature recommendation. The only downside to roasting a turkey in pieces? Youâll lose some of the drama that comes with ushering a whole roasted bird to the tableâbut who needs âoohs and ahhsâ when a chorus of âmmmsâ awaits? Additional reporting contributed by Zoe Denenberg.

item.title: Inside the largest airline lounge in America: United's massive new Houston club
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Inside the largest airline lounge in America: United's massive new Houston club United has fully embraced the "everything is bigger in Texas" mantra, as Houston is now home to not only the world's largest United Club, but also the largest airline lounge in the country. The new 54,000-square-foot United Club opens Thursday in the expanded Terminal B North concourse at George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH), which itself brings 22 new gates, a sensory room, play area, a host of new Houston-favorite restaurants and more. But the star of the show is unquestionably the massive United Club near Gate B11, with its outdoor terrace, Texas-style food and 800 seats spread across multiple zones. Here's a first look inside. Here's what you need to know about the new United Club at Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport Terminal B: - You can find the club postsecurity in the new Terminal B North addition, near Gate B11. - It's open 5:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily, beginning Oct. 22. - The 54,000-square-foot space is spread across a single level and includes a 1,350-square-foot outdoor terrace. - The new lounge is home to 800 seats, 11 private phone booths, two bars and two buffets. - It follows the same access rules as other United Clubs. The new Houston United Club isn't just the country's largest on paper; it actually feels that way when you are inside, too. In fact, during my preview visit, it almost felt like going down the rabbit hole in Alice in Wonderland, as the "rooms" within the lounge just kept flowing into one another. It is all one connected space, but there are multiple rooms within the United Club that feel quite distinct in both style and function. While it will certainly be different once the doors officially open and passengers fill the space, this area, with loungers overlooking the planes, had a calm, relaxing vibe during my media tour on Wednesday. Alternatively, this area of the lounge — with some tiered padded seating, an arcade game and a view of the terminal — felt like it had the potential to be a much livelier, family-friendly hangout spot. Those were just two of the multiple zones inside the lounge. Not only will the 800 seats inside the new club accommodate many passengers at once, but they will also have a choice of seat types and places to pass the time until their next flight. In a first for the Houston airport, this new United Club comes with a side of fresh air in the form of a 1,350-square-foot outdoor terrace overlooking the airfield. While Houston can certainly get warm, there are fans and sometimes a quick shot of fresh air on an airport day is all you need — even if it's in Houston's sweltering summer heat. And, of course, this may end up being the most popular spot in the lounge during Houston's milder times of the year. The new United Club's restrooms are also large. Even the stalls are spacious, which helps when your luggage has to take the restroom trip along with you. There were multiple private family restrooms in addition to the men's and women's rooms. The lounge also featured a private wellness room that looked to be designed for nursing, caring for a baby and pumping. Food and drinks at the new Houston United Club As mentioned, there are two bars and two buffets at this record-setting lounge — a testament to the work it takes to keep 800 people fed and happy. Food buffets at the new Houston United Club During my visit, both of the food buffets had the same items on offer: - Taqueria bar with meat, rice, beans, tortillas and taco fixings I tried pretty much everything, and while this was just a preview event, it was all genuinely enjoyable. I specifically loved the tres leches, but I'd look forward to every dish again in the future, which isn't always the case for airline lounge food. This mega-lounge has two full-service bars, and my favorite one may actually be the smaller of the two. The smaller bar, closest to the outdoor terrace, is called the Moonshot Bar — a nod to Houston's space history. In addition to the standard drink menu, this bar has copious tequila options. Of course, there is a list of standard, included options at both of the bars, too: - Bollicini Brut (sparkling wine) - Mainline wine blend (white) And there are complimentary soda machines, flavored water dispensers and fancy coffee machines with more options than I needed at 6 a.m. Plus, there are tons of candies and snacks. So who gets to come inside and enjoy this fancy new United Club? You're in the right place. There are a variety of ways to access a United Club, ranging from having the right credit card(s), getting one-time passes, purchasing a membership using miles or cash, having Star Alliance Gold status (when meeting certain other criteria) or flying on eligible premium-cabin tickets — all of which also require an eligible same-day boarding pass. United now also has two tiers of lounge access: individual membership and an All Access tier, which provides unlimited United Club access for the primary member and up to two guests, or one adult and two dependents under 18. If you want to learn all the nuances of scoring United Club access, I highly recommend reading our how-to guide. But, in my opinion, the easiest way in is to hold one of these United credit cards: - United Club℠ Card (see rates and fees): United Club membership for you and your eligible travel companions at all United Club locations and participating Star Alliance lounges worldwide. - United℠ Explorer Card (see rates and fees): Receive two one-time United Club passes each year. - United℠ Business Card (see rates and fees): Receive two one-time United Club passes each year. - United Club℠ Business Card*: Receive United Club membership for you and your eligible travel companions at all United Club locations and participating Star Alliance lounges worldwide *The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Lounge membership earned via a cobranded credit card includes entry for primary cardmembers, one guest and any dependents under 18, though cardmembers can unlock the All Access level of membership to increase the guest allowance. If you think frequent United Club visits are in your future, the pricier United Club cards are likely the way to go, as the $695 annual fee is still less than purchasing a membership outright. Otherwise, the two single-use United Club passes you get each year with the $95 United Explorer Card or the United Business Card might be enough to meet your lounging needs. Just know that sometimes United Clubs reach capacity and are unable to accept single-use passes until the crowds thin. The Terminal B expansion and the world's largest new United Club are massive upgrades for Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport. The lounge is not only undeniably spacious but also bright, airy and thoughtful — a place travelers will actually look forward to visiting, especially if they keep the enchiladas and tres leches on the menu. It is designed to handle many passengers who are either connecting through Terminal B or taking short- to medium-haul trips. And it joins the "United Club Fly" grab-and-go concept, also in Terminal B, to really make your time at the airport a much more enjoyable — and functional — part of your travel day. Related reading:
